en: Now, before we proceed to the Tailscale
step, there's one thing that can be
annoying.
On your Mac or Windows machine,
whenever you wanna connect, you have to
enter SSH and then max@
and then the IP, and you have to think about
adding
-i and enter the path to your key file. That
can be annoying.
So what you can do and might wanna do on
your Mac or Windows machine
is you can edit an SSH config file,
which you find in ~/ssh/config typically on
Mac
and in your user's username folder and then
also.ssh/config on Windows.
You can open that config file with any text
editor of your choice. Here I'm using Visual
Studio Code, but you can Use any plain text
editor, doesn't have to be anything fancy.
And then in there you add a new entry.
You may already have some entries in there,
but you add a new one which starts with host
and then any name of your choice, like for
example, VPS course for me, but that name is
totally up to you.
You will be able to connect to that VPS via
that name, so you might wanna keep it short
and easy to memorize.
Then
in a new line, you hit Tab to indent this
and there you add hostname. Hostname then
must be the IP address
So I'll grab my IP
and enter this here.
Then in a new line, still indented, you
enter your username with which you wanna
connect, Max in my case. Then you add a
port, 22, and then you add an identity file.
And here you point at your key file.
So in my case on a Mac, that is
~/.ssh,
and then in my case here, VPS course.
Or VPS course pub, you can point at the pub
file too, doesn't matter. It will
automatically find the private key file
assuming that you have the same base file
name.
On Windows, of course, it's your Windows
path, C colon and then backslashes,
users,
and then your username and so on. You have
that here,
but I'm on a Mac, so it's this.
And with this, you add a shortcut to your
VPS, so to say. So you can save this file
now on your Mac, on your Windows machine,
and now in there, if you just type ssh
vps-course and nothing else,
you'll connect with that user to that VPS
running on that IP. If the IP were to
change, of course, you would have to change
it in your SSH config file.
If you were to remove that entry, naturally,
you wouldn't be able to connect anymore. But
this is then simply a more convenient way of
quickly connecting to that machine.
